identification.summary: Storm-2603 is Microsoft's name for a threat actor first publicly described in July 2025 in connection with exploitation of on-premises SharePoint vulnerabilities (the 'ToolShell' chain), where Microsoft observed it stealing MachineKeys and, from 18 July 2025, deploying Warlock ransomware [S1][S2]. Microsoft says it has also seen the actor deploy LockBit ransomware in the past and that it cannot yet confidently assess the actor's objectives [S1]. Check Point traced related infrastructure to campaigns from March 2025 that delivered LockBit Black and Warlock/x2anylock ransomware [S3]. Other vendors track overlapping activity as GOLD SALEM (Sophos), CL-CRI-1040 (Palo Alto Unit 42) and Longlegs (Symantec) [S3][S4][S5].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft reports exploitation of the SharePoint flaws by actors as early as 7 July 2025 (all three named actors together; no Storm-2603-specific date) and Storm-2603 ransomware deployment from 18 July 2025 [S1]. Check Point links Storm-2603 infrastructure to campaigns dating back to March 2025 [S3]. Sophos lists related incidents from April 2025 [S4].
identification.notes: Vendor cluster boundaries differ and are not proven identical: Sophos GOLD SALEM, Unit 42 CL-CRI-1040 and Symantec Longlegs are described by secondary reporting as the same or overlapping activity [S3][S4][S5]. Microsoft states it found no links between Storm-2603 and other known Chinese threat actors, and distinguishes it from Linen Typhoon and Violet Typhoon, which exploited the same vulnerabilities [S1][S2]. Warlock is the ransomware name; Trend Micro has suggested it may be a rebrand of Anylock (.x2anylock extension) [S6].

attribution.confidence: Microsoft assesses with moderate confidence that Storm-2603 is a China-based threat actor and says it cannot confidently assess its objectives [S1]. Sophos reportedly said it lacks sufficient evidence to confirm the China-based attribution [S4]. Symantec, as reported by BleepingComputer, describes the actor (Longlegs) as China-linked [S5]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry on SharePoint exploitation and ransomware deployment [S1]. Check Point notes custom tooling (ak47c2 C2 framework, DLL sideloading) and earlier LockBit Black/Warlock activity [S3]. The basis for Microsoft's moderate-confidence China assessment is not detailed in the sources reviewed.

objectives: Unconfirmed. Microsoft says it cannot confidently assess objectives; it observed MachineKey theft and ransomware deployment (Warlock, previously LockBit) [S1]. Ransomware use and a leak site (about 60 victims published by September 2025 per Sophos) point to financial extortion [S4], but whether espionage or state tasking is involved is unverified.

sectors: Agriculture, finance and local government, business services, energy (nuclear) and industrial (Sophos incident table, April-August 2025) [S4]
regions: Portuguese- and Spanish-speaking countries in Europe, Africa and Latin America (Symantec, as reported October 2026) [S5]
North America, Europe and South America (Sophos leak-site observations) [S4]
targeting.notes: Initial access depends on unpatched on-premises SharePoint servers, so targeting follows exposure rather than a stated sector priority [S1][S5]. SharePoint Online in Microsoft 365 was reported as not affected [S2]. Victim names were not disclosed in the Symantec reporting [S5].

capabilities.summary: Initial access via CVE-2025-49706 and CVE-2025-49704 (ToolShell chain) against on-premises SharePoint, then the spinstall0.aspx web shell and theft of MachineKeys [S1]. Post-exploitation per Microsoft: whoami discovery, abuse of services.exe to disable Microsoft Defender, PsExec for SYSTEM and lateral movement, Impacket over WMI, Mimikatz against LSASS, scheduled tasks and IIS components loading malicious .NET assemblies for persistence, and Group Policy modification to push Warlock ransomware [S1]. Microsoft also lists an IIS backdoor (IIS_Server_dll.dll), SharpHostInfo and a fast reverse proxy (xd.exe) [S1]. Check Point describes a custom C2 framework the actor called ak47c2 with HTTP and DNS clients and reports multiple ransomware families, including LockBit Black and Warlock/x2anylock [S3]. Sophos reports Velociraptor misuse as ransomware precursor activity from mid-August 2025, VS Code tunnel C2 attempts and a vulnerable-driver (BYOVD) defense-evasion tool [S4]. Symantec, as reported, observed security tools disabled on at least 40 hosts in about two hours and Warlock launched on at least 33 hosts in one intrusion, plus DLL sideloading [S5].

campaigns.name: Earlier LockBit Black and Warlock/x2anylock activity
campaigns.summary: Check Point traced a domain tied to the SharePoint exploitation back to campaigns from March 2025, serving as C2 for DNS-tunneling and HTTP backdoors and delivering LockBit Black and Warlock/x2anylock ransomware.

campaigns.name: SharePoint ToolShell exploitation and Warlock deployment
campaigns.summary: Microsoft reported that Storm-2603 exploited on-premises SharePoint CVE-2025-49706 and CVE-2025-49704, deployed the spinstall0.aspx web shell, stole MachineKeys, and from 18 July 2025 deployed Warlock ransomware via Group Policy. Exploitation by the three named actors began as early as 7 July 2025. Microsoft's blog was published 22 July and updated 23 July 2025.

campaigns.name: Check Point publication on prior ransomware operations
campaigns.summary: On 31 July 2025 Check Point published 'Before ToolShell' describing the ak47c2 framework and multiple ransomware payloads used by Storm-2603.

campaigns.name: Velociraptor precursor activity
campaigns.summary: Sophos CTU identified legitimate Velociraptor DFIR tool use in likely ransomware precursor activity in mid-August 2025, attributed to GOLD SALEM.

campaigns.name: Warlock leak-site growth
campaigns.summary: Sophos reported about 60 victims published on the Warlock leak site by September 2025.

campaigns.name: Continued SharePoint exploitation against critical infrastructure
campaigns.summary: BleepingComputer (2 October 2026, reporting Symantec and Carbon Black) described Warlock/Longlegs intrusions at a water utility, telecom provider, regional government body and university in Europe, Africa and Latin America via SharePoint flaws, with web shells, DLL sideloading and ransomware on at least 33 hosts in one case.

diamond.adversary: Storm-2603, assessed by Microsoft with moderate confidence as China-based, with unassessed objectives; ransomware operator behavior with a Warlock leak site [S1][S4].
diamond.capability: ToolShell SharePoint exploitation, spinstall0.aspx web shell, MachineKey theft, ak47c2 C2, IIS backdoor, PsExec, Impacket, Mimikatz, GPO-based ransomware deployment, Velociraptor, BYOVD [S1][S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Microsoft lists C2 domains (update.updatemicfosoft.com, msupdate.updatemicfosoft.com), post-exploitation C2 IPs and an ngrok-hosted PowerShell delivery URL [S1]. Sophos reports a Cloudflare workers.dev domain for Velociraptor download [S4].
diamond.victim: Organizations with internet-facing on-premises SharePoint, including water, telecom, government, education, energy and industrial entities [S4][S5].
diamond.technology: On-premises SharePoint servers (ASP.NET machine keys, IIS), Windows domain environments using Group Policy, and security tooling that can be disabled via registry or vulnerable drivers [S1][S4].

gaps: Objectives and any state tasking are unconfirmed; Microsoft says it cannot confidently assess them [S1].
Basis for Microsoft's moderate-confidence China-based assessment is not public in the sources reviewed; Sophos reportedly lacks evidence to confirm it [S1][S4].

Cluster mapping among Storm-2603, GOLD SALEM, CL-CRI-1040 and Longlegs rests on vendor and press statements; primary Symantec, Unit 42 and Sophos reports could not be opened (hosts blocked from this environment) and were read only via search summaries.
The Check Point primary post could not be fetched; details come from search result summaries.
Warlock-Anylock rebrand claim (Trend Micro) and any Black Basta link are reported secondhand and unverified; the Security.com/Symantec article date (about August 2025) is approximate.
Victim names and counts are not public or are inconsistent across sources (leak-site count about 60 by September 2025; one aggregator cites 396 SharePoint servers across 145 organizations).
No government (CISA, DOJ) attribution or advisory specific to Storm-2603 was located.
Microsoft naming mapping and learn.microsoft.com naming page listed in the actor record were not opened in this pass.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-facing on-premises SharePoint servers and the Active Directory/Group Policy plane behind them are key terrain; ASP.NET machine keys let an intruder persist after patching [S1][S5]. STEP 2: The actor operates on exposure rather than sector, opportunistically hitting unpatched servers within days of disclosure; Microsoft saw ransomware begin on 18 July 2025 within about 11 days of first exploitation [S1]. STEP 3: Template is ToolShell exploit, web shell, MachineKey theft, Defender disablement, credential dumping, PsExec/Impacket lateral movement, then GPO-pushed ransomware, with DLL sideloading and tunnels for persistence [S1][S3][S4][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued extortion-style ransomware against organizations with unpatched or un-rotated SharePoint, including utilities and telecom [S5]. MDCOA, an assessment not stated in sources, is use of the same access against DoD-adjacent or critical-infrastructure hosts for disruption or espionage if objectives are state-directed, which is unconfirmed [S1]. Candidate indicators: spinstall*.aspx files, debug_dev.js, IIS_Server_dll.dll, xd.exe, unexpected GPO changes, Velociraptor or VS Code tunnel use, and Defender disabled through services.exe registry edits [S1][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track SharePoint exposure and patch/key-rotation status across mission-relevant enclaves, since patching alone does not remove stolen MachineKeys or persistence [S1][S5]. (2) Authorities: because attribution (state versus criminal) is unresolved, determine early whether response falls under defensive cyber operations, law-enforcement or DIB reporting channels; do not assume a state nexus [S1][S4]. (3) Mission assurance: ransomware deployed through Group Policy can reach many hosts in hours, so prepare offline backups and manual fallbacks for dependent mission systems [S1][S5]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DC3, the DIB CS program and sector partners, and note that Microsoft, Sophos, Symantec and Unit 42 use different names for overlapping activity [S3][S4][S5].
